idiom_name: multiple-assignment exchange (a, b = b, a) with the state behind one pointer or interface
implementation_notes: Go's assignment statement is the swap: the language evaluates the operands on the left and the expressions on the right, then assigns left to right, so `a, b = b, a` exchanges two values - the specification itself writes that line as "exchange a and b". There are no exceptions (only panics), so "non-throwing" becomes "cannot panic and allocates nothing": a type whose representation hides behind one pointer or interface value commits by rebinding that field, and because swapping struct values copies them, large state belongs behind a pointer. There is no swap protocol to implement (no ADL, no std::swap, no noexcept); where a rollback path must survive a panic, recover in a deferred function and restore the previous handle.
pitfalls: Multiple assignment is not atomic: another goroutine can observe one side updated and the other not; for shared state use a single atomic.Pointer[T]/atomic.Value or a mutex instead of two assignments.
Swapping struct values copies the whole struct including any array inside it, so exchange a pointer to the state rather than the state.
A swap through a nil pointer panics, so a non-throwing rollback path still has to guard its handles; recover() in a deferred function is Go's equivalent of the recovery branch.
An interface value is two words (type, data); reading one while another goroutine writes it without sync/atomic is a data race even though a single assignment is not torn.
